item.title: The Rise of Low Precision Floating Point
item.description: arXiv:2611.00301v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Floating point computing has dominated scientific computations since the 1950s because of its versatile ability to approximate real numbers with both sufficiently high precision and sufficiently great range. Since 1985, two specific formats have become standard across the industry, one with 32 bits which is adequate for many purposes and one with 64 bits which allows numbers with both much higher precision and much greater range for applications where these are needed. However, during the past decade, deep learning has come to dominate computation, and narrower floating point formats with lower precision and reduced range have steadily become more common. In this article we discuss this phenomenon, why it is happening, how various 16-bit, 8-bit and even 4-bit floating point formats have been developed, and efforts to standardize these formats.
item.dc:creator: Guy Lemieux, Michael L. Overton

item.title: Extensible Programmatic Specification of Finite Element Methods
item.description: arXiv:2611.01414v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite element methods (FEMs) are a powerful and ubiquitous tool for solving engineering problems. Experimenting with different finite elements can improve the quality and efficiency of solutions. In some cases, the wrong (but nonetheless most common) choice of finite element will produce solutions which converge to the wrong answer regardless of mesh resolution. However, in practice, the choice of finite element is not explored due to the complexity of re-deriving and re-implementing finite element methods. Trying a new finite element is challenging because practitioners must manually deduce formulas to use these elements and implement them within a potentially complex system. We address this problem by introducing ElementForge, a finite element system that is parametric over the literate mathematical specification of a finite element in a domain-specific language (DSL). The ElementForge compiler reasons about tensor spaces, tensors, and tensor bases from first principles to derive implementations of finite elements. The ElementForge compiler is able to automatically derive implementations of finite elements previously only derived by hand. Further, ElementForge minimally couples several key mathematical concepts, mainly tensor fields, mesh topologies, sparse tensors, and assembled finite element operators, to produce a complete finite element system that is parametric over the choice of element. Consequently, the elements derived by the compiler can be applied parametrically to new meshes, PDEs, and boundary conditions. We evaluate our system by implementing several simulations with different finite elements, demonstrating that our system can explore tradeoffs in generality, accuracy, speed, and representational complexity. For example, we are able to implement the Morley, Bell, Argyris, and Hermite like elements with less than 50 lines of code and use them all in a single simulation.
item.dc:creator: Theadora Fields Collin, Oded Stein, Gilbert Bernstein, Saman Amarasinghe

item.title: ARTA: Graph Combinatorial Optimization for Robust Interbeat Interval Estimation from Wearable Electrocardiogram Signals
item.description: arXiv:2611.00011v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate heart rate (HR) and interbeat interval (IBI) estimation from wearable electrocardiogram (ECG) is essential for continuous physiological monitoring, but motion artifacts can create false QRS-like peaks and obscure true R-peaks. Conventional detectors and local interval-repair rules process detections independently and may become unreliable when several consecutive beats are corrupted. We present ARTA (Artifact-Robust Temporal Alignment), a graph-based combinatorial framework that estimates the heartbeat sequence through constrained temporal optimization. ARTA combines candidates from multiple ECG detectors, represents them as nodes in a directed acyclic graph and connects candidates through physiologically plausible RR intervals. Candidate confidence uses detector agreement and local ECG quality, while history-dependent transition costs capture recent IBI consistency and a soft heart-rate prior. Beam-search dynamic programming selects a coherent low-cost path across the recording, suppressing false detections and recovering missed beats when plausible auxiliary candidates are available. On the IEEE Signal Processing Cup exercise dataset with electrode-motion artifacts from -2 to 12 dB, ARTA achieved an HR mean absolute error of 1.79 beats per minute, 54% lower than the strongest single-detector baseline, with 92.38% of windows within +/-5 beats per minute, an R-peak F1 score of 0.95, and an IBI mean absolute error of 6.52 ms. Cross-dataset evaluation on the European ST-T Database further assessed transfer to long clinical ambulatory recordings and a label-free reliability analysis examined conditional performance without using reference annotations for segment selection. ARTA is single-channel, training-free, interpretable and computationally lightweight, operating approximately 27 times faster than real time with peak memory below 2.1 MB in a single-thread CPU simulation.
item.dc:creator: Shovito Barua Soumma, Asiful Arefeen, Hassan Ghasemzadeh

item.title: Grassmann: The Coordinate-Independent Linear Algebra Programming Language
item.description: arXiv:2611.00182v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Scientists, engineers, and mathematicians often formulate algorithms using coordinate-independent linear algebra because its tools are composable and harder to misuse. For numerical processing, however, users must translate these ideas into coordinate-dependent array code. Most practitioners do so prematurely because tools such as NumPy lack coordinate-independent representations, while existing languages with such constructs do not model enough linear algebra for the situations where they matter. We propose Grassmann, a small language bridging coordinate-independent linear algebra and coordinate-dependent implementations. It uses dependent types, linear types, and partially (pseudo-)invertible computation to model situations arising in exterior algebra and differential geometry. It targets the linear algebra at a point on a manifold, a prerequisite for many specifications in scientific computing and computer graphics. A language for coordinates lets users move between these representations. We give a denotational semantics assigning meaning without coordinates and an operational semantics translating Grassmann to array code under a choice of coordinates. Our main metatheoretic result shows that operational evaluations agree with the denotational semantics under an arbitrary choice of coordinates. This models how practitioners translate linear algebra for computers and suggests an approach to algorithmic optimization at a high level of abstraction. Our optimized implementation generates code for exterior algebra operations with overheads no more than 10%.
item.dc:creator: Theadora Fields Collin, Gilbert Bernstein, Oded Stein, Saman Amarasinghe

item.title: Eunoia: Area-Proportional Euler and Venn Diagrams in Rust, Julia, Python, R, and JavaScript
item.description: arXiv:2611.02198v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Area-proportional Euler diagrams visualize sets and their intersections through regions whose areas represent their sizes. Because many set specifications have no exact geometric representation, constructing these diagrams requires numerical optimization and diagnostics that quantify the remaining discrepancies. Eunoia is a Rust library for fitting area-proportional Euler diagrams and constructing canonical Venn diagrams. It supports circles, ellipses, squares, and rectangles, computes region areas analytically, and provides exact analytical gradients for several shape families. Its fitting pipeline combines multidimensional scaling initialization with local refinement, global optimization when needed, and seeded restarts. Fitted layouts include residuals and goodness-of-fit statistics that help users assess how faithfully a diagram represents the data. Shared plotting routines extract region polygons, place labels, and pack unit glyphs and member names within regions. The same core implementation powers packages for R, Python, Julia, and JavaScript, a C interface, and a web application that fits diagrams entirely in the browser through WebAssembly. By centralizing fitting, geometry, diagnostics, and annotation in an independent library, Eunoia provides consistent set visualization across programming languages and interactive applications.
item.dc:creator: Johan Larsson, Nicole M. Lee

item.title: Multi-GPU Acceleration of Interface Problems in FEniCS, with Application to Cardiac Modeling
item.description: arXiv:2611.03181v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: GPU acceleration of finite element assembly is well established for standard formulations, but mixed-dimensional problems, in which volumetric subdomains are coupled via lower-dimensional interfaces, remain unsupported in automated frameworks such as FEniCS. We extend cuDOLFINx, a GPU-enabled extension of the DOLFINx finite element framework, to assemble such interface problems on GPUs while preserving the high-level FEniCS programming model. Combined with GPU-resident Krylov solvers and algebraic multigrid preconditioning, this enables end-to-end GPU execution of the EMI (Extracellular--Membrane--Intracellular) model, an elliptic interface problem from cardiac modeling in which many intracellular subdomains are coupled through membranes. We compare the GPU implementation against a CPU-based one through strong and weak scaling experiments on regular and realistic 3D cardiac geometries with up to 8000 cells and 22 million degrees of freedom. In terms of assembly, a single GH200 node is roughly equivalent to two 144-core CPU nodes in strong scaling, and to two to three nodes in weak scaling, depending on geometry. For the linear solver, performance depends on geometry, preconditioning, and problem scale. On the regular geometry, GPU advantages emerge mainly at larger problem sizes and node counts. On the realistic geometry, with the same algebraic multigrid preconditioner for both architectures, the GPU is faster at all tested scales. The implementation is available as open-source software and applies to other problems with interface coupling.
item.dc:creator: Edoardo Centofanti, Benjamin Pachev, Joshua Steyer, James D. Trotter, Pietro Benedusi

item.title: A GPU Engine for Sparse Matrix-Vector Products on $k^2$-Tree-Compressed Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.03610v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The $k^2$-tree is a compact representation of Boolean matrices: it stores the recursive hierarchy of their non-empty submatrices, with neither values nor coordinates, and serves rows and columns alike. Its traversal, however, locates the children of each node by rank queries, a chain of dependent irregular loads that leaves a GPU waiting on memory. We implement sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) on $k^2$-trees for the GPU. Since the traversal does not depend on the vector, the positions of the children are static: we descend the tree one level at a time and obtain them from a parallel prefix sum or from a sampled directory of about 0.1 bits per node. Descending in tiles bounds the temporary memory by the depth of the tree, so the device memory of a product is known before it runs. The same traversal computes right and left products, for one vector or a batch, over the plus-times, Boolean and tropical semirings. We evaluate the engine on an NVIDIA GB10 and an H100 with fourteen Wikidata, Software Heritage, web and social graphs of up to 1.2 billion edges, against cuSPARSE, a grammar-compressed GPU engine and a Boolean CSR. Our results show that the tree is 2.3-27x smaller than the CSR of cuSPARSE and that, with its last internal level cached, a product takes 0.7-2.4x the time of cuSPARSE on the right and 0.27-2.6x on the left. On a 1.2-billion-edge graph, a product needs 1.1 GB on the device, 9x less than cuSPARSE. The engine is memory bounded: the $k^2$-tree is the format of choice when device memory, not time, is the constraint.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli

item.title: Streaming Right Multiplication over Grammar-Compressed Matrices: A Memory-Bounded GPU Engine for Genotype and Graph Data
item.description: arXiv:2607.24971v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Grammar-compressed matrices store a matrix's non-zero structure as a RePair straight-line program (SLP), supporting matrix-vector products in time and space proportional to the compressed size. We target the regime where this is decisive on a GPU: when the uncompressed matrix exceeds device memory, so footprint (not floating-point throughput) is the binding constraint. Our SLP is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of out-degree 2, and the right product $y=Mx$ is a single bottom-up sweep (leaves to roots): a conflict-free gather. We make the grammar properly layered (every nonterminal child one level below its parent) via pass-through completion, which inserts identity nodes to carry values upward until consumed. This yields a streaming evaluation in which each level reads only the level below and writes the next, so the live set fits in two alternating read-only/write-only buffers instead of scaling with the whole grammar. On genotype matrices, where a polygenic score is exactly the right product $y=G\beta$, a CUDA implementation shows a clear space advantage: a device footprint 3.5 to 8 times smaller than a materialized cuSPARSE CSR baseline, single-vector times within a small factor of cuSPARSE, and consistently lower GPU energy. Because the sweep needs only an associative and commutative combine, the same engine evaluates any homomorphism into a commutative monoid over the grammar by swapping a small leaf/combine/emit policy; the same reachability sweep scales to a billion-edge Software Heritage graph (261 TB dense, 21 times smaller serialized than cuSPARSE's CSR). We frame this as an algorithm-engineering case study: structural metrics (depth, live-set width, completion cost) are measured, architecture-independent grammar properties, whereas time and energy are profiled on a single board.
item.dc:creator: Francesco Tosoni, Gabriele Mencagli

item.title: DRO: A Python Library for Distributionally Robust Optimization in Machine Learning
item.description: arXiv:2505.23565v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce dro, an open-source Python library for distributionally robust optimization (DRO) for regression and classification problems. The library implements 15 DRO formulations and 9 backbone models, enabling 85 distinct DRO methods. Furthermore, dro is compatible with both scikit-learn and PyTorch through a unified interface, and uses approximation techniques to reduce runtime for some computationally demanding formulations. Comprehensive documentation is available at https://python-dro.org.
item.dc:creator: Tianyu Wang, Jiashuo Liu, Henry Lam, Hongseok Namkoong, Jose Blanchet
